title: Epistle of Barnabas
subtitle: an early Christian reading of the Law as figures of Christ, and the two ways of light and darkness
lead: The Epistle of Barnabas is a letter-treatise written by an unnamed Christian teacher to believers he had taught and loved, at "the end of the first or beginning of the second century" in Lake's judgment. Its aim, in Kirsopp Lake's words, "is to warn Christians against a Judaistic conception of the Old Testament." The writer wants his readers to have "perfect knowledge" along with their faith, and he finds that knowledge in a figurative reading of Israel's Scriptures. God never wanted sacrifices and fasts (2–3). The scapegoat and the red heifer were figures of the suffering Christ (7–8). True circumcision is of the heart, and the 318 men Abraham circumcised spell out Jesus and the cross (9). The food laws teach how to live, not what to eat (10). The Sabbath points to a coming age, and Christians keep the eighth day, the day Jesus rose (15). God's real temple is the believer's heart (16).

The letter's sharpest claim is about the covenant. It says the covenant belongs to Christians, because Israel lost it at Sinai when Moses broke the tablets over the golden calf (4:6–8; 14:1–4), and it says of circumcision in the flesh: "But the circumcision they have trusted in has been done away with. For he said that circumcision was not to be done in the flesh. But they went against it, because an evil angel was tricking them." (9:4). This conflicts with Paul, who says the covenants still belong to Israel and that God's gifts and call cannot be taken back (Romans 9:4–5; 11:28–29), and the Catholic Church has said that the Jews must not be presented "as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures" (Nostra Aetate 4). The letter is translated here plainly and in full, and the notes say where it parts from the Bible. Its last chapters change tone and give a form of the Two Ways, the way of light and the way of darkness, close to the opening of the Didache (18–20).

Outside the Bible. The Epistle of Barnabas is not in the Bible of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Ethiopian, Anglican, Reformed or Baptist churches. It once came close in Egypt: Clement of Alexandria quoted it as the work of "the Apostle Barnabas," Origen called it a "general" (catholic) epistle, and the great fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus copies it right after Revelation, "without any suggestion that it belonged to a different category of books" (Lake). But Eusebius put it among the rejected writings (Church History 3.25.4), Jerome says it "is reckoned among the apocryphal writings," and Lake reports that its ascription to Paul's companion Barnabas is "generally regarded as impossible to accept."
facts: Not in the New Testament of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Ethiopian, Anglican, Reformed or Baptist churches (Trent; Reid, 1908; the EOTC list; Article VI; Westminster and the 1689 Confession). It stood at the edge of the canon: after Revelation in Codex Sinaiticus (Lake), near the end of the list of books in Codex Claromontanus, between Jude and Revelation (Westcott), among the disputed books in the Stichometry of Nicephorus (Westcott), and among the rejected writings in Eusebius (Church History 3.25.4).

Unnamed. Clement of Alexandria calls him "the Apostle Barnabas" (Stromata 2.6) and "one of the seventy, and a fellow-worker of Paul" (2.20); Jerome too ascribes the letter to Barnabas (Lives of Illustrious Men 6). Lake: the tradition is "generally regarded as impossible to accept." Ladeuze infers from 1:2, 4 and 21:7, 9 that the writer had "exercised the office of a didaskalos" (teacher) in the church he writes to, though he says he writes "not as a teacher" (1:8; 4:9).

"Doubtful" (Lake), and known to Clement of Alexandria about AD 200. Lake reports two arguments from the text: the ten kings of 4:4–5 read as Roman emperors, which would put it "well within the limits of the first century," and the rebuilding of the Temple in 16:3–4 read as the events of AD 132. "Neither theory is quite satisfactory, but neither date is in itself impossible"; it "no doubt belongs to the end of the first or beginning of the second century." Westcott sees in 16:3–4 "an allusion to the destruction of the Jewish Temple" (AD 70). Ladeuze (1907) dates it to AD 130–131; the Jewish Encyclopedia (1902) ties it to the time of the Bar Kokhba revolt.

Unknown. Lake: "either a general treatise or was intended for some community in which Alexandrian ideas prevailed"; Ladeuze argues for Alexandria from the allegorical method and from the fact that before the fourth century only the Alexandrians knew it.

A letter in form, a treatise in substance: a chain of quotations from the Greek Old Testament, often joined from several books, each followed by its figurative meaning, then a moral catechism, the Two Ways (18–20).
Greek. An old Latin version survives for chapters 1–17 only.

The Greek printed by Kirsopp Lake (Loeb Classical Library, 1912), from Codex Sinaiticus (fourth century), the Codex Constantinopolitanus (AD 1056), eight late Greek manuscripts that lack the start of the letter, and the Latin version (Lake).
authorship: Nothing of the writer's name. He greets his readers as sons and daughters, in peace (1:1), calls them "children" and "brothers," and twice says he writes "not as a teacher": once "but as one of you" (1:8), once "but as fits someone who loves you" (4:9); at 4:6 he again asks them "as one of you." He says he is passing on a share of what he received (1:5).

From about AD 200 the letter goes under the name of Barnabas, the Levite from Cyprus who traveled with Paul (Acts 4:36–37; 13:1–3). Clement of Alexandria quotes it as the words of "the Apostle Barnabas" (Stromata 2.6) and of "the apostolic Barnabas (and he was one of the seventy, and a fellow-worker of Paul)" (2.20). Jerome lists it under Barnabas: he "wrote one Epistle, valuable for the edification of the church, which is reckoned among the apocryphal writings" (Lives of Illustrious Men 6). Westcott notes that Origen and Eusebius are silent on who wrote it.
Why scholars set the tradition aside

Lake: the tradition is "generally regarded as impossible to accept, though it is convenient to continue to use the title." Westcott: "From its contents it seems unlikely that it was written by a companion of Apostles, and a Levite," and the letter contains, in 16:3–4, "an allusion to the destruction of the Jewish Temple." Ladeuze, a Catholic scholar, finds that the writer "is not always familiar with the Mosaic rites" (on chapter 7) and constantly sets himself and his readers against the Jews, so that it is "impossible to believe" he or most of his readers were Jews by birth. The Jewish Encyclopedia takes the opposite view of his knowledge, finding "an astonishing familiarity with the Jewish rites," and reports Güdemann's view that the writer "seems to have been a converted Jew." Either way, the name Barnabas belongs to the tradition, not to the letter.

Westcott suggests that a writing "known to be of the Apostolic age" might "very naturally be attributed to the 'Apostle' in default of any other tradition," and that the supposed link between Barnabas of Cyprus and Alexandria, where the letter first gained credit, made the guess more natural. On the man himself, see the topic Barnabas.

audience.to: Christians whom the writer had taught and loved and from whom he was now apart (1:2–5; 21:7–9), apparently a community where Greek allegorical reading of Scripture was at home: "some community in which Alexandrian ideas prevailed," in Lake's words, though neither its place nor the writer's can be defined. The writer greets them as sons and daughters (1:1), so women may have been among the readers. They were Gentile believers, Ladeuze argues: the writer sets himself and them against the Jews throughout, and says that before they believed, their heart was a house full of idolatry (16:7). Some among them seem to have been saying that the covenant was both theirs and ours, that is, shared by the Jews and the Christians (4:6).
audience.why: To give them "perfect knowledge" along with faith (1:5): a way of reading Israel's Scriptures that sees Christ and the church in every law and rite, so that they would not dash themselves against "their law" like newcomers, nor think the covenant still belonged to those who kept the Law as written (3:6; 4:6–8). The writer also expects the end soon (4:3, 9; 21:3) and wants his readers ready, so he closes with the Two Ways as a rule of life (18–20). Knowing the readers matters. The letter is not a missionary tract aimed at Jews but teaching for Christians, which is why it can speak of "those people" so harshly: they are outside the room. That makes its claims easier for its first readers to accept and harder for later readers to excuse.
views: A real community, or a treatise?

Lake leaves open whether it is "a general treatise" or meant for one community. Ladeuze thinks the letter form "is not entirely fictitious": the writer had been a teacher in a particular church and was now away from it (1:2, 4; 21:7, 9).

Ladeuze reads the letter as "the peaceful speculations of a catechist": Judaism is discussed "only in the abstract," with no sign that the readers were about to adopt the Law. The Jewish Encyclopedia reads it as a bitter product of the struggle between Jews and Christians in the time of the Bar Kokhba revolt (AD 132–135).
If 16:3–4 refers to Hadrian's rebuilding at Jerusalem, the readers lived about AD 130–132 (Ladeuze); if the ten kings of 4:4–5 are emperors, a generation earlier. Lake keeps both open.

outline: Greeting and purpose: faith, and with it perfect knowledge
God does not want sacrifices and fasts, but a broken heart and justice
The last stumbling block: Daniel's ten kingdoms; the covenant is ours, lost by them at Sinai; many called, few chosen
Why the Lord suffered in the flesh; the stone, and the land flowing with milk and honey as the new creation
The fast, the two goats and the scarlet wool; the red heifer and the children who sprinkle
Circumcision of the ears and heart; an evil angel misled them; the 318 men as Jesus and the cross
The food laws as lessons about people to avoid and to join
Water and the cross foretold: Moses' raised arms, the bronze serpent, Joshua son of Nun called Jesus, David's Lord
Which people is the heir: Rebekah's two peoples, Ephraim and Manasseh, Abraham; the covenant given to us through Jesus
The Sabbath: six days as six thousand years, God's true rest, and the eighth day
The Temple: torn down and rebuilt by enemies; the true temple in the heart
The end of the first part
The Two Ways: the way of light and the way of darkness, with angels over each
Closing: keep the commandments, the day is near; farewell

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Asks when and where the letter was written (the ten kings of 4:4–5, the rebuilding of 16:3–4, Alexandria), who the writer was, what sources he used (collections of Old Testament proof texts, the Two Ways), and how the manuscripts preserve it.

lenses.name: Jewish practice and the parting of the ways
lenses.desc: Sets what Barnabas says Jews did and believed beside Jewish sources (the scapegoat and the red heifer beside the Mishnah, the hopes of rebuilding the Temple in Hadrian's time) and asks what the letter shows about Jews and Christians drawing apart, and how Jewish scholars have read it.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Reads the letter beside the New Testament: Hebrews on sacrifice, covenant and rest; Paul on circumcision, the Law and Abraham (Romans 2–4, 9–11; Galatians 3–4); the Gospel sayings it quotes (4:14; 5:9); 1 Peter 2 on the stone.

lenses.name: Typology and allegory
lenses.desc: Studies the method itself: the "knowledge" (1:5; 9:8), the figure (Greek typos), the counting of letters (9:8), the animal lore of chapter 10, Philo's kind of allegory, and how later Christian readers took up or judged this way of reading.

lenses.name: Christian reception
lenses.desc: Follows the letter's later life: Clement of Alexandria and Origen, Codex Sinaiticus and the canon lists, and how today's churches judge its teaching on Israel and the Law.

sections.b:
The Plain English Translation is made for this site from the Greek printed by Kirsopp Lake in the Loeb Apostolic Fathers (vol. 1, 1912), as digitized by First1KGreek and corrected against the scans of Lake's page. Where Lake's text departs from all his manuscripts, the variants call it "Lake's text"; every place where the Plain English Translation departs from Lake, and every reading in his notes that changes the meaning, has a variant entry. The greeting is 1:1; there is no 1:0.

The writer quotes the Greek Old Testament constantly, freely, and sometimes joining two or three verses into one, and some of his "Scriptures" match no known book. Where his Greek matches a verse the site has translated from the Hebrew, the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording; where it differs, it translates what he wrote, and a note says how it differs. He seldom says "the Jews": he says "they," "those people" or "the first people," and the translation keeps his words as they stand.

The letter never names its writer. Its title, "Epistle of Barnabas," is in the manuscripts and in Clement of Alexandria, about AD 200, who quotes it as the work of "the Apostle Barnabas" (Stromata 2.6). Barnabas was the Levite from Cyprus who sold a field for the church, brought Paul to the apostles and traveled with him (Acts 4:36–37; 9:27; 13:2). Lake reports that the attribution is "generally regarded as impossible to accept," and Westcott argues from the letter's contents: "From its contents it seems unlikely that it was written by a companion of Apostles, and a Levite," and it contains, in 16:3–4, "an allusion to the destruction of the Jewish Temple." The name stays because it is the one the letter has always had.

The letter itself gives two clues, and Lake calls the date "doubtful."

  • The ten kings (4:4–5). The writer quotes Daniel on ten kingdoms and a small king who will humble three of them (Daniel 7:7–8, 24). If he meant the Roman emperors, counted to his own day, the letter is from "well within the limits of the first century" (Lake); but, Lake notes, "there is no unanimity as to the exact manner in which the number of the ten Emperors is to be reached." Ladeuze objects that nothing proves the writer thought the prophecy already fulfilled, or that he did not read the ten as kingdoms rather than kings.
  • The Temple torn down and rebuilt (16:3–4). "It is happening. For because they went to war, it was torn down by their enemies. Now the very servants of their enemies will build it up again." Westcott reads this as "an allusion to the destruction of the Jewish Temple" in AD 70, and Lake reports that the rebuilding "is supposed to refer to the events of 132 A.D." Ladeuze dates the letter to 130–131 from it, and links 9:4 to Hadrian's ban on circumcision. The Jewish Encyclopedia's article on Hadrian notes that the verse's "interpretation is disputed among scholars" but that it "seems to indicate that the Jews expected the pagans to rebuild the Temple"; its article on the letter reads chapter 16 as saying the Temple is "to be rebuilt only in a spiritual sense by the Christians," and sets the whole letter in the time when Jewish Christians "still clung to the Jewish nation in its last struggle against Rome under Bar Kokba" (AD 132–135).

Lake's judgment: "Neither theory is quite satisfactory, but neither date is in itself impossible," and the letter "no doubt belongs to the end of the first or beginning of the second century."

Lake places the readers in "some community in which Alexandrian ideas prevailed," and says the writer "carries a symbolical exegesis as far as did Philo," the Jewish thinker of Alexandria who read the Law as allegory, "indeed he goes farther." Ladeuze argues for an Alexandrian writer: the method is Alexandrian, and "up to the fourth century only the Alexandrians were acquainted with it, and in their Church the epistle attained to the honour of being publicly read." The writers who quote it before the fourth century, Clement of Alexandria and Origen, both taught at Alexandria. Lake himself stops short of Ladeuze: "it is not possible to define either its destination, or the locality from which it was written, with any greater accuracy."

The writer's key word is "knowledge" (Greek gnōsis), the deeper understanding that God gives to see what the Scriptures really mean (1:5; 6:9; 9:8). It is not yet the secret knowledge of the later Gnostic groups, as the note at 1:5 explains. His tool is the figure (Greek typos): Isaac offered on the altar, the cursed goat driven into the wilderness, the scarlet wool among the thorns, the red heifer, Moses' outstretched arms and the bronze serpent are all figures of Jesus and his cross (7:3, 7, 10–11; 8:1; 12:2, 5–6). He also reads hidden meanings in numbers and letters: the 318 men of Abraham's household are the Greek numerals for IH (the first letters of Jesus) and T (the shape of the cross) (9:7–8). And he reads the food laws as moral lessons, drawing on animal lore about the hare, the hyena and the weasel (10:6–8).

Ladeuze calls the letter's allegory "exaggerated": the writer "goes far beyond St. Paul the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, and St. Ignatius." Lake goes further, with 9:4 in view: the writer "apparently denies any literal significance at all to the commands of the Law," and "the literal exegesis of the ceremonial law is to him a device of an evil angel who deceived the Jews." The New Testament reads the Law as a shadow of good things to come and Christ as its fulfillment (Hebrews 10:1; Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 10:4); Barnabas reads it as never meant to be kept as written. The topics Types and Shadows and Allegorical Reading follow the method through later Christian writers.

This is the hardest part of the letter, and the site gives it plainly. The writer warns his readers against people "who pile up sins by saying, 'The covenant is theirs and ours'" (4:6). Then: "Yes, it is ours. Those people, though, lost it once and for all in the following way, when Moses had only just received it. For the Scripture says: "And Moses was on the mountain fasting forty days and forty nights. And he received the covenant from the Lord, tablets of stone written by the finger of the Lord's hand."" (4:7). And: "But they turned to idols and lost it. For this is what the Lord says: "Moses, Moses, go down quickly, because your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, have acted lawlessly." And Moses understood, and he threw the two tablets out of his hands. And their covenant was smashed, so that the covenant of Jesus the Beloved might be sealed into our hearts in the hope that faith in him gives." (4:8; Exodus 32:19). In 13–14 he argues from Rebekah's twins, from Jacob's blessing of Ephraim before Manasseh, and from Abraham, that the younger people, the church, is the heir, and that the covenant was given through Jesus to us, because they were not worthy to receive it (14:1–5). Of circumcision in the flesh he says that "an evil angel was tricking them" (9:4). Their Sabbaths and their Temple were not what God wanted (15; 16).

Readers have weighed how far the letter goes. Ladeuze writes that "according to many scholars" it teaches "that the Jews never had a covenant with God, that circumcision was the work of the Devil," but thinks it more exact to say that the writer condemns a "purely material observance," so that in his view "the Jews never received the divine covenant because they never understood its nature." The Jewish Encyclopedia sees in it "an anti-Judaic spirit of great bitterness."

Measured by the Bible, the letter's claim conflicts with Paul. Paul says that to the Israelites belong "the covenants" and the promises (Romans 9:4–5), that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2), and that God's gifts and call cannot be taken back (Romans 11:29). The Catholic Church, in the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965), recalls those words of Romans 9 and says that "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures." The site's cards on the church and Israel are at Galatians 6 and Acts 28, and the topics Christian Anti-Judaism and the Bible and The Church and Israel follow the question through history.

sections.h: The Two Ways and the Didache
sections.b:
Chapters 18–20 turn from figures to commandments: there are two ways of teaching and power, the way of light and the way of darkness, with angels of God over the one and angels of Satan over the other (18:1). Most of the commandments of chapter 19 and the vices of chapter 20 appear, in another order, in the first part of the Didache (Didache 1–5). Lake, in his introduction to the Didache, sets out the three possibilities: Barnabas used the Didache, the Didache used Barnabas, or both used a common source. "The matter is not clear, but probably the majority of scholars incline to the last view, and many think that the common source ... was a Jewish pre-Christian document, used for catechetical purposes."

The Latin version stops at the end of chapter 17, so it has no Two Ways. Lake: "the question (perhaps insoluble) arises whether the Latin has omitted it, or the Greek interpolated it. At present the general opinion is in favour of the former view." The Jewish Encyclopedia took the other view, that the Two Ways "betrays an altogether different spirit, and was probably attached to it by some copyist at a much later time." Ladeuze, for his part, saw the Two Ways as borrowed "from another document (the Didache or its source)" by the writer himself.

sections.h: Codex Sinaiticus and the early readers
sections.b:
The complete Greek text was first known from Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible of the fourth century, published by Tischendorf in 1862 (Jewish Encyclopedia). There the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas "follow the books of the New Testament" (Ladeuze). Lake stresses that it stands there "not, as is sometimes said, as an appendix, but following immediately after the Apocalypse, without any suggestion that it belonged to a different category of books." Lake: Barnabas, "like I. Clement and Hermas, became canonical in some circles."

Clement of Alexandria quotes it often and with respect (Stromata 2.6, 2.15, 2.20, 5.8, 5.10), and Eusebius says he commented on it in his Outlines (Hypotyposes) along with the disputed books of the New Testament (Church History 6.14.1) and used it among "the disputed Scriptures" (6.13.6). Origen calls it "the general Epistle of Barnabas" (Against Celsus 1.63). Ladeuze judges that the way Clement and Origen refer to it shows that "about the year A.D. 200, even in Alexandria the Epistle of Barnabas was not regarded by everyone as an inspired writing."

sections.h: The Latin and the eight G manuscripts
sections.b: Lake's witnesses are four. Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, fourth century). The Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), written in 1056 and found by Bryennios in 1875, the same manuscript that holds 1 Clement and the Didache. Eight Greek manuscripts (G) that all descend from one damaged copy: in it the end of Polycarp to the Philippians and the start of Barnabas had been lost, and a copyist ran Polycarp's chapter 9 straight on into the fifth chapter of Barnabas, so these manuscripts lack the opening chapters (Lake; Ladeuze says they lack chapters 1 to the first half of 5:7). Ladeuze notes that up to 1843 these eight were the only Greek copies known in the West. And a Latin version in one manuscript at St Petersburg, which stops at the end of chapter 17 (Lake); Ladeuze dates the version perhaps to the end of the fourth century and calls it "a very free one." So chapters 1–4 rest on ℵ, C and the Latin; chapters 5–17 on all four; chapters 18–21 on the Greek alone.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Barnabas reads Exodus 32 the way Paul reads Exodus 34
spec.body: Both Barnabas and Paul build an argument about the covenant on the stone tablets at Sinai. Paul uses the second giving of the tablets, when Moses' face shone and he wore a veil (Exodus 34:29–35), to say that a veil lies over the reading of the old covenant until a person turns to the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:7–16). Barnabas uses the first giving, when Moses broke the tablets over the golden calf (Exodus 32:19), to say that the covenant was lost then and there (4:7–8; 14:2–4). My suggestion is that the difference in the chosen scene carries the difference in the teaching: Paul's veil can be lifted, so Israel's story continues (compare Romans 11:25–26), while Barnabas's broken tablets end the story for Israel. Lake, Ladeuze, Westcott and the Jewish Encyclopedia, the writers opened for this page, do not compare the two scenes, and I know of no published comparison from what was opened; it rests on the verses named.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the letter's two halves answer one question
spec.body: Chapters 1–17 ask what the commandments of the Law mean, and answer that they were never meant literally. Chapters 18–20 then give commandments meant to be kept exactly as written: do not murder a child, do not commit adultery, share everything with your neighbor (19:4–8). Whoever joined the two, the writer or a later copyist, the effect is that the letter does not end in pure allegory: it replaces a literal Law it rejects with a literal moral code it accepts. Read this way, the Two Ways is not an odd appendix but the letter's answer to its own question, what the people of the new covenant are to do. This touches the published debate over whether the Two Ways belonged to the letter from the start (Lake; the Jewish Encyclopedia; Ladeuze; see "The Two Ways and the Didache"), but those writers ask where the chapters came from; reading the two halves as question and answer is mine.

prompts: On a rocky mountain slope, a bearded man in a rough robe lifts two stone tablets over his head and is about to throw them down; far below in a valley a crowd dances around a small golden calf on a pedestal; beside the scene, in the margin, a Christian teacher in a plain tunic writes on a scroll for a group of listeners, pointing up at the tablets. Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll, sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like cave paintings, Greek letters along the border, a few bold flat shapes in the manner of modern paper cut-outs; soft, torn edges fading into the parchment, never a hard rectangle.
The two ways of light and darkness (Barnabas 18)

A single road forks into two paths: one climbs toward a rising sun with a tall, quiet angel of light standing beside it and a few walkers in plain clothes helping one another; the other descends into shadow, watched over by a dark winged figure, where small figures quarrel and grasp at coins. Style: hand-sketched onto a parchment scroll in ink and soft watercolor washes, the bright path in gold ochre and the dark one in charcoal, cave-painting animals at the roadside, flat modern shapes for the sky; soft edges, no frame.

Abraham, an old man with a long beard, stands before a long line of men of his household; above them float three large Greek letters, T, I and H, drawn like carved stone, with the T shaped as a cross and the I and H glowing faintly; a scribe below counts on a wax tablet. Style: sketched onto an ancient scroll in sepia ink and charcoal, with hieroglyph-like register lines and ochre pigment, mixed with bold flat modern shapes; soft, faded edges.
reading: Kirsopp Lake, The Apostolic Fathers, vol. 1, Loeb Classical Library (1912)
Greek text with facing English and a short introduction; public domain, and the base text and English check text of this site.
Paulin Ladeuze, "Epistle of Barnabas," The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907)
A short Catholic survey of the text, the allegory, the date and the Alexandrian setting.
Crawford Howell Toy and Kaufmann Kohler, "Barnabas, Joses," The Jewish Encyclopedia (1902)
A Jewish reading of the letter's knowledge of the rites and of its hostility to Judaism.

canon.summary: The Epistle of Barnabas is an anonymous Christian treatise from the end of the first or the beginning of the second century (Lake) that reads the Law of Moses as figures of Christ. It is not in the Bible of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Ethiopian, Anglican, Reformed or Baptist churches. In Egypt it came close to the canon: Clement of Alexandria quoted it as the work of the apostle Barnabas, and Codex Sinaiticus copies it right after Revelation; but Eusebius counted it among the rejected writings, and Lake reports that its ascription to Paul's companion is "generally regarded as impossible to accept."
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of the New Testament books does not include it. Ladeuze, in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), treats it as an early writing important for "the history of the Canon of the Scriptures" and argues for an Alexandrian origin. He reports that "according to many scholars" it teaches that "the Jews never had a covenant with God," so that "he represents a unique point of view in the struggle against Judaism," and then corrects them: "It might be said more exactly that he condemns the exercise of worship by the Jews in its entirety because in his opinion, the Jews did not know how to rise to the spiritual and typical meaning" of the Law. The Church's own teaching on the Jews, in Nostra Aetate 4 (1965), rejects the idea that the Jews are "rejected or accursed by God."

Not in the New Testament as Reid (1908) describes it: the Eastern Orthodox churches "have a New Testament identical with the Catholic." This page found no Orthodox church statement that names the Epistle of Barnabas. One Byzantine list does name it: the Stichometry appended to the Chronography of Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople (806–814), puts it among the disputed books of the New Testament, with the Revelation of John, the Apocalypse of Peter and the Gospel of the Hebrews (Westcott, Appendix D). That list is a table of books attached to a chronicle, not a decision of the church, and Westcott thought it "probable that he borrowed it as it stands from some earlier writer" (458).
Not Scripture. The church's list of its 35 New Testament books does not include it.
Not Scripture. Article VI receives "all the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received"; the Epistle of Barnabas is not one of them.

Westcott (1896) wrote that "the Lutheran Church has no recognised definition of Canonicity, and no express list of the Sacred Books," and that usage settled the place of the disputed books. This page found no Lutheran statement that names the Epistle of Barnabas. On the letter's hostility to Judaism, the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) declared that "we recognize in anti-Semitism a contradiction and an affront to the Gospel."

Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament, "given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life" (1.2), and says that "the books commonly called Apocrypha" are "no part of the canon of Scripture" (1.3). It does not mention early Christian writings such as Barnabas; the letter is simply not in its list.

Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 New Testament books (1.2) and, like Westminster, rejects "the books commonly called Apocrypha" (1.3). It does not mention Barnabas, which is not in its list.

provenance.h: A Christian teacher, at the turn of the second century
provenance.b: An unnamed teacher wrote it in Greek to believers he had taught, at "the end of the first or beginning of the second century" in Lake's judgment (see "When was it written?"). Ladeuze argues that he wrote at Alexandria; Lake says only that the letter was for readers among whom "Alexandrian ideas prevailed," and that its place cannot be fixed. He drew on the Greek Old Testament, often in combined or freely worded quotations, on some writings outside the 66 ("Enoch" at 4:3; a Scripture close to 1 Enoch 89 at 16:5, as the site's 1 Enoch notes show; probably 4 Ezra at 12:1, as Ladeuze suggests), and on the Two Ways (18–20).

Before the fourth century it is known only from Alexandrian writers (Ladeuze). Clement of Alexandria quotes it by name several times and commented on it (Eusebius, Church History 6.14.1); Origen calls it a general epistle. It was copied into Codex Sinaiticus after Revelation in the fourth century. The list of books written into Codex Claromontanus, between Philemon and Hebrews, ends with "The Epistle of Barnabas, the Apocalypse of John, the Acts of the Apostles, the Shepherd, the Acts of Paul, the Revelation of Peter" (Westcott, 528–529); Westcott calls the list "obviously imperfect and corrupt," and in his printing of it Barnabas, with the Shepherd, the Acts of Paul and the Revelation of Peter, carries a mark that, in Tischendorf's note, a fairly late hand added (Appendix D, 576).

In the West the letter survived in a Latin version of chapters 1–17 and in eight late Greek manuscripts that lacked its opening chapters (Lake; Ladeuze). The whole Greek text came to light only with Tischendorf's publication of Codex Sinaiticus in 1862 and Bryennios's discovery of the Constantinople manuscript in 1875 (Jewish Encyclopedia).

• The prophets against empty ritual: Isaiah 1:11–14, Isaiah 58:4–10 and Jeremiah 7:22–23 (2–3), read as saying that God never wanted the rites at all.
  • The Law's rites: the Day of Atonement and the scapegoat (Leviticus 16), the red heifer (Numbers 19), circumcision (Genesis 17), the food laws (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14), the Sabbath (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11).
  • Israel's story: the golden calf (Exodus 32), Moses' arms and the bronze serpent (Exodus 17:8–13; Numbers 21:6–9), Rebekah's twins and Jacob's blessing (Genesis 25:21–23; 48:9–19).
  • Gospel sayings: many called, few chosen, introduced with "as it is written" (4:14; compare Matthew 22:14), and Jesus' call of sinners (5:9; compare Matthew 9:13).

rejected_why.b: The letter's claim to Barnabas rests only on the tradition, not on anything the letter says, and its contents tell against it (Westcott; Lake). Even at Alexandria, where it was most honored, Ladeuze judges that about AD 200 it "was not regarded by everyone as an inspired writing." Westcott held that the honor paid to Clement, Barnabas and Hermas, short of the canon, "becomes an indirect evidence of the implicit reverence paid to the Apostolic words, and of the Apostolic basis of the Canon" (522).

Eusebius sorted the books into the accepted, the disputed, and the rejected, and put "the extant epistle of Barnabas" with the Shepherd, the Acts of Paul, the Apocalypse of Peter and the Teachings of the Apostles among "the rejected writings," adding that all these "may be reckoned among the disputed books" because many church writers knew them (Church History 3.25.4–6). Athanasius's list of the New Testament (367) does not include it, nor his list of books for new believers (Festal Letter 39). Jerome says the letter "is reckoned among the apocryphal writings" (Lives of Illustrious Men 6), and Westcott that "in Jerome's time it was still read among the Apocryphal Scriptures." The Stichometry of Nicephorus counts it among the disputed books of the New Testament (Westcott). Where it does stand in a list, as in Codex Claromontanus, Westcott warns that such lists "are no more than tables of contents" (529).

rejected_why.h: Its teaching on Israel and the Law
rejected_why.b: The ancient lists give no reasons. Measured by the New Testament (this is Claude's analysis; see the reliability section), its teaching conflicts on three points: it says the covenant was never Israel's after Sinai, that God never meant the Law to be kept as written, and that an evil angel misled the Jews (4:6–8; 9:4; 14:1–4). The New Testament says the covenants still belong to Israel (Romans 9:4–5), that God's call is irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and that the Law is holy and its commandment holy, righteous and good (Romans 7:12), a shadow pointing to Christ, not a deception (Hebrews 10:1).

cited_in.b: Barnabas warns his readers not to be found, as it is written, many called but few chosen, introducing the words with "as it is written." They match Jesus' saying in Matthew 22:14. Ladeuze takes this as citing the Gospel of Matthew "as Scripture"; Westcott thought it possible that the writer referred the phrase "rightly or wrongly" to some Old Testament Scripture, while Sanday and Cunningham, as Westcott reports, inclined to Matthew. If it is Matthew, a Gospel saying is here introduced as Scripture.

Barnabas says Jesus chose as apostles men lawless beyond all sin, to show that he came to call not the righteous but sinners, the words of Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17. Origen later answered the pagan critic Celsus on this very passage of "the general Epistle of Barnabas" (Against Celsus 1.63).

Hebrews and Barnabas both quote the prophets and Psalms against sacrifice and say that Christ has ended the old offerings. Hebrews reads them as a shadow of good things to come (Hebrews 10:1); Barnabas as things God never asked for (2:4–6). Ladeuze judges that Barnabas goes "far beyond" Hebrews in allegory. No literary dependence either way is shown here.

Here the link is a conflict, not a borrowing. Paul lists "the covenants" among Israel's gifts; Barnabas says the covenant is ours and that Israel lost it at Sinai (4:6–8; 14:4). See the section "The Jews and the covenant."
Like 1 Peter and Romans 9:33, Barnabas joins the stone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16) with the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22) and reads both of Christ (6:2–4).

2 Peter 3:8 and Barnabas both use Psalm 90:4, that with the Lord a day is as a thousand years. 2 Peter uses it to explain the Lord's delay; Barnabas to count six thousand years for the six days of creation, before God's rest (15:4–5). The site's note at 2 Peter 3:8 already makes this link.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how some Christians read Israel's Scriptures in the generation after the apostles, and to how sharply Christians and Jews had drawn apart by the time it was written, the Epistle of Barnabas is very valuable. Its text is fairly well preserved in three Greek lines of witnesses and an early Latin version, though the first chapters rest on few copies. Its claims about Jewish practice must be checked against Jewish sources, which sometimes agree and sometimes do not. Measured by the 66 books it agrees on Christ and the moral life, goes far beyond them in allegory, and plainly conflicts with them on Israel, the covenant and the Law.

sections.h: 1. A witness to early Christian reading: high
sections.b: The letter shows a Christian teacher, writing for readers among whom "Alexandrian ideas prevailed" (Lake), using the Greek Old Testament as a book about Christ in every line, with proof texts joined from several prophets, figures, numbers and moral allegory. It shows the Two Ways in Christian use, early Christian hope for the end, and the keeping of the eighth day as the day of Jesus' resurrection: "That is why we also keep the eighth day with gladness. It is the day on which Jesus rose from the dead, and after he had been revealed, went up into heaven." (15:9). It shows a Christian community that defined itself against the synagogue, and so it is also a witness to early Christian hostility to Judaism, which is why it matters to read it with care.

The whole Greek survives in Codex Sinaiticus (fourth century) and the Constantinople manuscript (1056); eight late Greek copies lack the first chapters; the Latin covers chapters 1–17 freely (Lake; Ladeuze). Lake's notes show places where the witnesses differ in sense, and at 1:6 he says "the text of this whole passage is confused." Chapters 1–4 and 18–21 rest on fewer witnesses than the rest. Whether the Two Ways belonged to the letter from the start is argued (see "The Two Ways and the Didache").

The letter's title claims Barnabas, and Lake reports that the claim is "generally regarded as impossible to accept." Its statements about the rites are partly confirmed and partly its own. For the heifer's ashes "taken up by boys, who sprinkled the people," the Jewish Encyclopedia compares Mishnah Parah 3:3; but the Mishnah there has children riding to the Shiloah spring, filling stone cups with water, and, on reaching the Temple Mount, a child putting the ashes into the water (Mishnah Parah 3:2–3); it does not have children gathering the ashes into jars or sprinkling the people, as Barnabas 8:1 does. Other details have no known source, which led Ladeuze to think the writer "not always familiar with the Mosaic rites." Its animal lore in chapter 10 is ancient natural history, not fact. Its dates rest on how two passages are read (4:4–5; 16:3–4).

• Matches: Jesus is the Lord who suffered in the flesh for our sins, rose and went up to heaven (5:1–7; 15:9); God wants a broken heart and justice more than sacrifice (2:10; Psalm 51:17; Isaiah 58:6–7); circumcision of the heart (9:1–5; Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4; Romans 2:29); the believer as God's temple (16:8–10; 1 Corinthians 3:16); the moral commands of the Two Ways (19), including the protection of the unborn and newborn child (19:5).
  • Goes beyond: it reads almost every rite of the Law as a figure of Christ, far past the New Testament's own uses of typology, and reads numbers and letters (9:8); it counts six thousand years before the end (15:4); it quotes "Scriptures" that no known book contains (6:13; 7:4; 12:1).
  • Conflicts: it says that the covenant was never Israel's after Sinai (4:6–8; 14:1–4), where Romans 9:4–5 and 11:28–29 say the covenants and God's call remain Israel's; it says that God never wanted the sacrifices and fasts he commanded (2–3), where the Law gives them as God's commands (Leviticus 1; 16) and the prophets condemn rites without justice, not the rites themselves; and it says that keeping circumcision in the flesh came from an evil angel (9:4), where Genesis 17:9–14 gives it as God's covenant sign and Paul calls the Law holy (Romans 7:12). How the churches answer: the Catholic Church has said that the Jews must not be presented as rejected by God "as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures" (Nostra Aetate 4), and the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) calls anti-Semitism "a contradiction and an affront to the Gospel" without discussing Barnabas or the covenant. For the Orthodox, Ethiopian, Anglican, Reformed and Baptist churches this page found no statement that addresses these claims.

how_to_read.b: The Epistle of Barnabas is not in the Bible of any church named on this page. Read it as a window into one early Christian teacher's way of reading the Old Testament, not as a word of God to you.

how_to_read.h: Test its readings by the Bible
how_to_read.b: Some of its figures are found in the New Testament or became common Christian readings (the bronze serpent, Moses' raised arms, the eighth day). Others are its own (the 318, the hyena). Where it says the Law was never meant to be kept, or that Israel lost the covenant, the notes mark the conflict with Paul: read Romans 9–11 beside it.

The letter's words about "those people" belong to the long history of Christian contempt for Jews that the topic Christian Anti-Judaism and the Bible traces. Do not soften them, and do not repeat them. The Catholic Church (Nostra Aetate 4) and the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) have rejected that contempt in their own words.
Chapters 18–20 are an early Christian moral catechism, shared with the Didache. They can be read with profit by any Christian as a summary of the commandments and the love of neighbor.
